title: How the Electoral College Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain the U.S. Electoral College: why it exists (compromise between a popular vote and Congress choosing the president), how electors are allocated (538 total, two per senator plus House seats, three for D.C. under the 23rd Amendment), who can be an elector, the winner-take-all system used by 48 states versus the district systems in Maine and Nebraska, and faithless electors. They review historical elections decided against the popular vote (1824 Adams/Jackson, 1876 Hayes/Tilden, 1888 Harrison/Cleveland, 2000 Bush/Gore), the 2000 Florida recount, the reform proposals and public opinion on abolishing it, and a voter-access concern in Ohio. The episode closes with a trivia event announcement in New York City and listener mail from Jack Mead in England asking for a podcast-withdrawal support group.
topics: Stuff You Should Know trivia event New York

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to the Electoral College
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about Chuck's cold and the topic, noting that many people do not realize they are voting for electors rather than directly for a candidate.

segments.title: Origins and the compromise behind the Electoral College
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Founders' distrust of a direct popular vote and of Congress choosing the president, and the resulting compromise. They note election timing: the Tuesday after the first Monday in November, and electors voting the first Monday after the second Wednesday in December.

segments.title: How electors are allocated and who they are
segments.summary: There are 538 electors: two per senator plus House seats per state, with three for D.C. from the 23rd Amendment of 1961. Voters choose electors, who are often not on the ballot. Electors' names and addresses are public in some states.

segments.title: Qualifications and nomination of electors
segments.summary: Electors are usually nominated by state party committees, often as rewards for party service. The Constitution sets few requirements; members of Congress are barred, as are people who have engaged in insurrection or rebellion, and holders of high trust or profit positions.

segments.title: Winner-take-all versus district systems and faithless electors
segments.summary: Forty-eight states use winner-take-all, so the slate of electors for the popular-vote winner gets all the state's electoral votes. Maine and Nebraska use a district system: two votes go to the statewide winner and the rest by congressional district. Faithless electors who vote against their pledge risk fines, removal and loss of party support.

segments.title: Elections where the winner lost the popular vote
segments.summary: The hosts cover elections where the winner lost the popular vote: 1824 (John Quincy Adams over Andrew Jackson, decided by the House under the Twelfth Amendment), 1876 (Hayes over Tilden, with Colorado's votes), and 1888 (Harrison over Cleveland, with Southern states voting as a bloc on the tariff). Other notes include Burr and Jefferson's 1800 tie.

segments.title: The 2000 election, Florida, and the Gore electoral count
segments.summary: Josh recalls the 2000 election night and the Florida recount, decided by less than a few hundred votes, with hanging chads and disputed counties. Florida's winner-take-all rule gave Bush the electoral votes needed. Gore, as vice president and Senate president, had to read the electoral count that defeated him.

segments.title: Criticism, reform proposals, and voter turnout
segments.summary: Critics say the system discourages turnout in non-swing states. Defenders argue it weights populous states. Over 700 reform proposals have been introduced in two hundred years, and polls show public dislike of the system; the ABA favored abolition while political scientists generally supported it.

segments.title: Ohio early voting restrictions
segments.summary: The hosts discuss an Ohio Secretary of State decision to give blue counties shorter early-voting hours and no weekend voting compared with red counties, and their objections to inconsistent voting procedures within a state.

segments.title: Trivia event announcement in New York City
segments.summary: The hosts announce a trivia event in New York City on Friday, October 12, and ask listeners for venue suggestions.
topics: Stuff You Should Know live trivia

segments.title: Listener mail from Jack Mead about podcast withdrawal
segments.summary: Listener Jack Mead from England writes about binge-listening to the show and missing it between episodes, and suggests a special episode with the hosts' wives. The hosts ask listeners for ideas on a withdrawal support group.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The episode closes with the sign-off and a repeat of the camera sponsor line.
